title: Being with the dying
hook: presence, prayer and quiet at a bedside
tomorrow: why lay a white cloth over the coffin at a Catholic funeral?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph, who never says a word in the Gospels, and the three names for a happy death: Jesus, Mary, Joseph. Today, the room where those names get said.
screen: `JESUS, MARY, JOSEPH.` → `THE ROOM WHERE THEY'RE SAID.`

segments.voice: A bedside has its own sounds: a machine humming, a cart going by in the hall, someone else's TV through the wall. And beside someone who is dying, the hardest sound can be the silence. What do you say? Maybe nothing much. The Catholic answer is older and simpler than a speech: stay.

On his last night, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus doesn't ask his friends for advice. He asks for company, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death; stay you here, and watch." They fall asleep, and he comes back and asks again. The next day, John writes: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." No speech is recorded from her there. She stands. Here's one to tell a friend: an old Latin hymn about that moment is named for her posture, Stabat Mater, the mother was standing. At a Catholic bedside, staying looks plain. A hand held. A wet cloth on dry lips. A rosary said softly, or just the end of the Hail Mary, over and over. A call to the priest, if it hasn't happened. And quiet, without hurrying to fill it. The Church has its own prayers for this hour, commending the person to God as they go. But the first gift needs no words at all. You don't have to fix anything. Stay beside.
screen: `STAY YOU HERE, AND WATCH.` · `HIS MOTHER STOOD BY THE CROSS.` · `A HAND, A ROSARY, THE QUIET.` · `NOTHING TO FIX.` · then, large: `STAY BESIDE.`

segments.voice: Learn one line by heart now, so it's there when you need it: the end of the Hail Mary, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Say it slowly, out loud, three times. Then sit with the name of someone you'd want to say it beside.
Being with the dying. Presence, prayer and quiet at a bedside, staying when there's nothing left to fix.
Your line: stay beside, the way Mary stood by the cross and simply stayed. Good night.

howItsDone: Catholics keep vigil with the dying at home or in the hospital, praying the rosary or the Hail Mary, calling a priest for the anointing and viaticum, and using the Church's prayers of commendation for the dying.

chat.says: sitting with Doña Carmen. she's not really awake. i have no idea what to say. do i just leave?
options: Stay. Hold her hand, pray a Hail Mary softly. Jesus asked his friends to stay, not talk.
Leave and come back when she's awake. Visits only help if she can talk with you.
Fill the quiet with stories so it isn't awkward. Silence makes it feel worse.
chat.meaning: In Gethsemane, Jesus asked his friends to stay and watch, and Mary stood by the cross. Presence and quiet prayer are the gift.

Gethsemane.meaning: the garden where Jesus prayed on the night before he died

Stabat Mater.meaning: an old Latin hymn: the mother was standing

Hail Mary.meaning: a prayer to Mary that begins with the angel's greeting

rosary.meaning: a string of beads for praying Hail Marys and other prayers

notes: Mark 14:34 and John 19:25 quoted from Douay-Rheims (Challoner); confirm exact wording.
'No speech is recorded from her there' (Mary at the cross in John 19:25–27): claim about the text; confirm.
Stabat Mater named for Mary's posture ('the mother was standing'): the Latin meaning of the hymn's first words. Confirm.
The Hail Mary's last line is said in the practice without quotation marks (a traditional prayer, not a new one). The Church's prayers of commendation are described, not quoted.
For parents: the lesson describes a deathbed gently (a held hand, a wet cloth on dry lips, quiet). Doña Carmen dies after this day; the death itself is not described.
